---
title: "Disruption"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-01-30"
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

In layman's terms, ECT is often compared to a "system reboot" of a computer. A standard reboot sequence begins by sending termination signals to all active processes and resetting hardware registers to their default states. Subsequently, the operating system kernel reloads and system services restart to achieve a "clean state," purged of prior errors. While the biological complexity of the human brain defies direct comparison, this metaphor provides an insightful image of the ECT process. The seizure effectively acts as a global termination signal for aberrant neural activity, dismantling hyperconnectivity within or between network modules. This acute disruption precipitates profound shifts in network architecture, facilitating the pruning of maladaptive connections and the rewiring of functional networks, much like the re-initialization of system drivers. This metaphor has implicitly influenced theoretical models of ECT and is increasingly substantiated by empirical evidence of post-ECT network dynamics.

Even if the seizure is analogous to the act of pressing the reset switch, it may not be a sufficient condition for therapeutic success. The critical determinant is rather the integrity of the subsequent "cleaning" and "reconfiguration". The modern paradigm has thus pivoted from maximizing seizure duration toward optimizing "seizure adequacy," characterized by robust postictal suppression [@AZUMA2007; @FrancisTaylor2020]. This shift acknowledges that the therapeutic process occurs largely after the ictus has ceased. This conceptual evolution has unfolded very gradually; historically, it was even postulated that ECT worked by inducing retrograde amnesia, effectively "erasing" traumatic memory traces [@Cameron1960; @Miller1967]. This was followed by the theory that ECT exerts its therapeutic action via an anticonvulsant mechanism [@Duthie2015]. Regardless of the specific mechanism proposed, the generalized seizure was long considered the *sine qua non* of ECT efficacy. However, the ascendancy of the neuroplasticity hypothesis [@Duman2006; @Laroy2025] has challenged this dogma [@Lisanby2007; @Deng2024].

Pressing the reset switch would inevitably entail collateral damages. The disruptive impact of ECT is more readily observed through immediate cognitive deficits. For instance, Gbyl et al.[@Gbyl2024] reported significant reductions in functional connectivity between the hippocampus and posterior DMN hubs, specifically the precuneus and posterior cingulate cortex. This suggests a breakdown in the temporal synchrony required for memory. Historically, transient cognitive impairment was deemed an inevitable tradeoff for ECT efficacy. However, as the focus has shifted away from seizure intensity per se, there is a growing expectation that meticulous optimization of stimulation parameters can secure therapeutic adequacy without precipitating memory deficits [@Weiner1984; @Sackeim2007].

After the ictal phase, the first observable phenomenon is postictal suppression [@azuma2007;@langroudi2023]. This represents an acute phase of network inhibition and bioelectric silence. It seems to be driven by a surge of GABA and adenosine that effectively blocks presynaptic glutamate release. This stage is followed by postictal slowing which is characterized by a pronounced increase in the power of delta and theta rhythms [@fink1957; @kolbeinsson1988; @rosn1987]. During this period, thalamocortical re-coupling is delayed, and synaptic downscaling occurs to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio [@leaver2022]. This period ends with the initiation of plasticity window. It is within this temporal window that metabolic recovery aligns with the induction of neurotrophic factors like BDNF, facilitating the recalibration of neural networks and the restoration of excitatory-inhibitory balance.

Recent optical neuroimaging evidence enables us to reinterpret these phenomena through the lens of "Cortical Spreading Depolarization (CSD)" [@Rosenthal2025]. CSD is a wave of massive neuronal depolarization that travels slowly across the cortex, silencing bioelectric activity in its wake. This event represents a profound physiological reset characterized by the breakdown of transmembrane ion gradients and a surge in extracellular glutamate and adenosine. This also triggers a multiphasic hemodynamic signature: an initial hyperemic surge driven by the metabolic needs of massive depolarization, followed by a transient vasoconstriction, and finally a prolonged rebound hyperemia. Crucially, it is this coordinated alteration of neuronal activity that may drive the upregulation of immediate early genes (*c-Fos*, *Arc*) and plasticity-related proteins (*Homer1*), effectively converting the acute disruption into a long-term neurotrophic signal [@KaastrupMller2015; @Dyrvig2015; @DellOrco2023].

The metabolic sequelae of ECT can be indexed by changes in N-acetylaspartate (NAA), the most abundant amino acid–derived metabolite in the brain and a widely accepted marker of neuronal viability and mitochondrial integrity [@Moffett2007]. Transient reductions in NAA within the anterior cingulate cortex have been observed 7–14 days following a course of ECT, with subsequent normalization at 6-month follow-up [@erchinger2023]. This reversible decline likely reflects a temporary disruption of neuronal function rather than irreversible structural damage.

ECT’s acute disruptive effect can be framed as a violent deformation of the attractor landscape. From the perspective of the critical roaming hypothesis ([DOI: 10.64898/2025.12.29.696846](https://doi.org/10.64898/2025.12.29.696846)), this is not a single escape event but a process of continuous exploration. Post-ECT fluctuations in arousal and neuromodulatory tone can be modeled as stochastic drifts in control parameters (e.g., synaptic gain and excitability) that drive the system across critical transition lines. This facilitates a stochastic exploration of connectivity patterns, effectively widening the reachable state space and increasing the probability of the network settling into a healthier attractor basin.
